overview: This two-page file contains a cross-reference sheet concerning the proposed marriage of Tatsuni Iwahashi, an American consular clerk at Dairen, to a Japanese subject, together with an apparently unrelated Far Eastern Affairs memorandum reporting tightened foreign-exchange controls in the Kwantung Leased Territory. The marriage sheet directs researchers to Despatch No. 47 of December 2, 1940, which proposed obtaining a legally unassailable marriage and documenting precisely what occurred; the referenced despatch itself is not present. The second document notes that all remittances abroad, regardless of size, had become subject to special permits.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 47 on Tatsuni Iwahashi's proposed marriage
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a Dairen despatch about arranging and precisely documenting the legally valid marriage of an American consular clerk to a Japanese subject.
subfiles.summary: Tatsuni Iwahashi, described as an American clerk at the consulate, wished to marry a Japanese subject on or about December 6, 1940. The referenced paper offered suggestions for securing a legally unassailable marriage and recording exactly what took place. The sheet identifies the missing original as Despatch No. 47, dated December 2, 1940, from Dairen and associated with Chase.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Kwantung foreign-exchange restrictions
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum records Dairen's report that foreign-exchange regulations in the Kwantung Leased Territory had been tightened.
subfiles.summary: Referring to Dairen telegram No. 31 of August 5, 1940, the Division of Far Eastern Affairs noted that the territory's foreign-exchange regulations had become more rigid. Every remittance abroad, however small, now required a special permit. The initials and routing notation indicate internal departmental circulation or review.

interest: The file is useful for studying the practical legal difficulties of marriages between American consular personnel and Japanese subjects in Japanese-controlled Dairen, although the substantive despatch survives here only as a cross-reference. Its wording shows official concern not merely with legal validity but also with producing a precise record of the ceremony or procedure. The juxtaposition of this reference with a memorandum on increasingly strict remittance controls also illustrates the heterogeneous character—and occasional filing incongruities—of State Department decimal-file bundles.
